evidence: Thermometers made quantitative investigation possible, meaning that thermal processes could be studied using numerical measurements.
Thermal conduction is heat transfer through a material from warmer parts to cooler parts.
They introduced heat capacity, which describes the energy needed to raise a body's temperature by one degree under stated conditions without a change of state.
They also developed a quantitative theory of thermal conduction, one that makes predictions with numbers.
Mechanical work transfers energy when a force moves something, and experiments showed that continued rubbing could warm a body as mechanical energy was supplied.
The textbook also points to steam cooling as it does work in an engine: some of its energy leaves as work, rather than necessarily as heat passed to another body.
findingResolutions.assessment: The quantitative gloss is correctly placed at its first occurrence in prose 2, so this authorized addition directly closes the readability finding rather than expanding the assignment. Conduction and heat capacity now have concrete inline meanings; heat capacity includes the no-change-of-state and stated-setup conditions. The work gloss is tied to the original rubbing and working-steam examples. Continued rubbing requires supplied energy, and the steam example explicitly identifies energy leaving as work. The text retains the no-energy-from-nothing warning and does not invent a named experiment, numerical exercise, figure or apparatus detail.

evidence: The textbook describes a result established by the middle of the nineteenth century: experiments demonstrated the quantitative equivalence of mechanical work and heat transfer.
This means that the amounts transferred by working on a body and by heating it can be compared using the same measure of energy.
It does not mean that an engine can convert all the heat it receives into work.
Heat and work are two ways of transferring energy, not substances contained in an object.
findingResolutions.assessment: The repair restores both the source-attributed mid-nineteenth-century timing and the experimentally measurable equivalence, with a plain explanation of the common energy measure. Heat and mechanical work remain transfer mechanisms, internal energy remains distinct from transferred heat, and supplying heat is said to be able to increase internal energy rather than always raising temperature. The explicit engine caveat prevents equivalence from implying complete conversion of received heat into work.
